                      fig.align = "center", out.width = "85%")
find_proj_root <- function(path = getwd()) {
  path <- normalizePath(path)
  repeat {
    if (length(list.files(path, pattern = "\\.Rproj$"))) return(path)
    parent <- dirname(path)
    if (parent == path) stop("No .Rproj file found above ", getwd())
    path <- parent
  }
}

knitr::opts_knit$set(root.dir = proj_root)

```{r load}
source(file.path(proj_root, "R", "utils_data.R"))

library(knitr)

# ---- Settings for this notebook -------------------------------------------
FIRST_YEAR <- 1996   # first feature year: needs five earlier years of history (1991-95)
LAST_YEAR  <- 2024   # last feature year: its label needs 2025, the last complete year
TRAIN_LAST <- 2016   # train on feature years up to 2016, test on 2017-2024

full <- read_csv(file.path(paths$processed, "rq1_district_quarter_full.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  filter(ta != "Chatham Islands Territory")
range(full$yq)
```

# Purpose

**Research question 3:** *Will a district's consents rise or fall next year?*

This is a **binary classification** problem. For each district and year we know what happened up to the end of that
year, and we predict whether the number of new dwellings consented **next** year will be higher (rise) or not (fall).
The pitch proposed logistic regression, linear discriminant analysis (LDA) and a classification tree.

This notebook builds the table (one row per district and year), defines the label, builds the features, and
explores them. Models are in Step 2.

# One row per district and year

We add up the quarterly district table from RQ1 into **calendar years**. 1990 is incomplete (it starts in April)
and 2026 is incomplete (it ends in June), so complete years run from 1991 to 2025. As in RQ2, the Chatham Islands
are left out: about three new dwellings a year give a label that is mostly noise, with many years of no change.

```{r annual}
annual <- full |>
  filter(year >= 1991, year <= 2025) |>
  group_by(ta, region, island, is_city, year) |>
  summarise(quarters  = n(),
            dwellings = sum(dwell_n),
            houses    = sum(houses_n),
            h1        = sum(dwell_n[quarter <= 2]),       # January-June
            h2        = sum(dwell_n[quarter >= 3]),       # July-December
            alt_real  = sum(resid_alt_val * real_factor),
            nonres_real = sum(nonres_new_val * real_factor),
            dwell_per_1000 = dwell_per_1000[quarter == 4],  # the 12 months to December
            .groups = "drop")
stopifnot(all(annual$quarters == 4))
c(districts = n_distinct(annual$ta), years = n_distinct(annual$year), rows = nrow(annual))
```

# The label: rise or fall next year

$$\text{rise}_{d,t} = 1 \text{ if new dwellings}_{d,t+1} > \text{new dwellings}_{d,t}, \text{ otherwise } 0.$$

We use **new dwellings** (all types), the headline count of the consents data. A year with *exactly* the same number
as the year before counts as "not rising". Those ties are rare and only happen in very small districts.

```{r label}
annual <- annual |>
  group_by(ta) |>
  arrange(year, .by_group = TRUE) |>
  mutate(next_dwellings = lead(dwellings),
         rise = as.integer(next_dwellings > dwellings),
         tie  = next_dwellings == dwellings) |>
  ungroup()

annual |> filter(!is.na(rise)) |>
  summarise(rows = n(), share_rising = mean(rise), ties = sum(tie), share_ties = mean(tie)) |> kable(digits = 3)
```

**Observation.** Overall, rises and falls are close to balanced, so accuracy is a fair measure and no re-weighting of
classes is needed. Ties are under 2% of rows.

# Features: what is known at the end of year *t*

Every feature uses information available on 31 December of year *t*, so the model could have been used at that
date to predict year *t* + 1. Nothing from year *t* + 1 is used.

| Feature | Definition | Why it might predict next year |
|---|---|---|
| `log_dwellings` | log(1 + new dwellings in year *t*) | Size; small districts swing more |
| `growth_1y` | log change in dwellings from *t* − 1 to *t* | Momentum (a rise continues) or reversal (a rise is followed by a fall) |
| `growth_2y` | log change from *t* − 2 to *t* | Longer momentum |
| `dev_5y` | log(dwellings in *t*) minus the average log of the previous five years | Above its usual level, a district may fall back (mean reversion) |
| `h2_vs_h1` | log(dwellings July–December ÷ January–June) in year *t* | Direction at the end of the year: a strong second half points upwards |
| `alt_growth` | log change in real residential alteration value | Spending on existing homes as a sign of local demand |
| `nonres_growth` | log change in real non-residential value | Local business investment |
| `multiunit_share` | share of new dwellings that are not stand-alone houses | Apartment and townhouse projects come in lumps, so they make counts jumpy |
| `dwell_per_1000` | new dwellings per 1,000 residents in the year | Building intensity relative to the population |
| `nat_growth_1y` | the same as `growth_1y` for New Zealand as a whole | National cycle |
| `nat_dev_5y` | the same as `dev_5y` for New Zealand | Is the country above its usual level? |
| `nat_h2_vs_h1` | the same as `h2_vs_h1` for New Zealand | National direction at the end of the year |

`+ 1` inside the logs avoids log(0) for districts with no dwellings in a year or half-year.

```{r features}
lg <- function(x) log(x + 1)
mean_prev5 <- function(x) (lag(x, 1) + lag(x, 2) + lag(x, 3) + lag(x, 4) + lag(x, 5)) / 5

nat <- annual |>
  group_by(year) |>
  summarise(nat_dwellings = sum(dwellings), nat_h1 = sum(h1), nat_h2 = sum(h2), .groups = "drop") |>
  arrange(year) |>
  mutate(nat_growth_1y = lg(nat_dwellings) - lag(lg(nat_dwellings)),
         nat_dev_5y    = lg(nat_dwellings) - mean_prev5(lg(nat_dwellings)),
         nat_h2_vs_h1  = log(nat_h2 / nat_h1),
         nat_rise_next = as.integer(lead(nat_dwellings) > nat_dwellings))

rq3 <- annual |>
  group_by(ta) |>
  arrange(year, .by_group = TRUE) |>
  mutate(log_dwellings   = lg(dwellings),
         growth_1y       = log_dwellings - lag(log_dwellings, 1),
         growth_2y       = log_dwellings - lag(log_dwellings, 2),
         dev_5y          = log_dwellings - mean_prev5(log_dwellings),
         h2_vs_h1        = lg(h2) - lg(h1),
         alt_growth      = lg(alt_real) - lag(lg(alt_real)),
         nonres_growth   = lg(nonres_real) - lag(lg(nonres_real)),
         multiunit_share = if_else(dwellings > 0, 1 - houses / dwellings, 0)) |>
  ungroup() |>
  left_join(nat |> select(year, nat_growth_1y, nat_dev_5y, nat_h2_vs_h1, nat_rise_next), by = "year")

# 2025 rows: features are known, the outcome (2026) is not. Kept aside for forecasting (used by the app).
forecast <- rq3 |> filter(year == LAST_YEAR + 1)

rq3 <- rq3 |>
  filter(year >= FIRST_YEAR, year <= LAST_YEAR) |>
  mutate(split = if_else(year <= TRAIN_LAST, "train", "test"))

features <- c("log_dwellings", "growth_1y", "growth_2y", "dev_5y", "h2_vs_h1", "alt_growth", "nonres_growth",
              "multiunit_share", "dwell_per_1000", "nat_growth_1y", "nat_dev_5y", "nat_h2_vs_h1")
c(rows = nrow(rq3), missing_values = sum(is.na(rq3[c(features, "rise")])))
rq3 |> count(split, name = "rows") |>
  left_join(rq3 |> group_by(split) |> summarise(years = paste(min(year), "to", max(year)), share_rising = mean(rise)),
            by = "split") |> kable(digits = 3, caption = "Train and test district-years")
```

**Observation.** Every row has every feature, because rows start in 1996: `dev_5y` needs five earlier years
(1991–95), and `dwell_per_1000` starts in 1996. The pitch counted 1,742 training rows from 1991. Starting in 1996
gives fewer but complete rows (no imputation). The split is by time again: train on feature years 1996–2016 (labels
1997–2017), test on 2017–2024 (labels 2018–2025).

# How much does the year matter?

```{r by-year, fig.height = 3.8}
by_year <- rq3 |> group_by(year, split) |>
  summarise(share_rising = mean(rise), nat_rise = first(nat_rise_next), .groups = "drop")

p_year <- ggplot(by_year, aes(year + 1, share_rising)) +
  annotate("rect", xmin = TRAIN_LAST + 1.5, xmax = Inf, ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf, alpha = 0.1, fill = "#e07a1f") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.5, colour = "grey60") +
  geom_col(aes(fill = factor(nat_rise, labels = c("NZ fell", "NZ rose")))) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("NZ fell" = "#2a6f97", "NZ rose" = "#e76f51")) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  labs(title = "Share of districts whose new dwellings rose, by year",
       subtitle = "Colour = whether New Zealand's total rose that year. Shaded = test years.",
       x = "Year of the outcome (t + 1)", y = "Districts rising", fill = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "top")
save_fig(p_year, "fig01_share_rising_by_year", dir = paths$fig_rq3, height = 3.8)

# how much of the label's variation is "which year it is"?
summary(lm(rise ~ factor(year), data = rq3 |> filter(split == "train")))$r.squared
```

**Observation.** The share of districts rising swings enormously from year to year: from about 12% (2009, during the
global financial crisis) to about 88% (2021, the post-COVID boom). Districts mostly rise and fall **together**, with
the national building cycle. When New Zealand as a whole rose (red), most districts rose; when it fell (blue), most
fell.

Knowing only *which year* it is explains about `r fmt_pct(summary(lm(rise ~ factor(year), data = rq3 |> filter(split == "train")))$r.squared, 0)`
of the variation in the label (R² of a linear model on year alone). That is a lot for a 0/1 label. It means a large
part of the problem is predicting the **national** direction next year, which no district feature can know for
certain. This puts a ceiling on how well any model can do, and it is why the national features are included.

The test years are harder than the training years in one respect: they include the sharp turn after the 2021 boom: 88% of
districts rose in 2021, but under 25% rose in 2023 and in 2024.

# Features against the label

```{r feature-boxplots, fig.height = 6}
p_box <- rq3 |> filter(split == "train") |>
  select(rise, all_of(features)) |>
  pivot_longer(-rise, names_to = "feature") |>
  mutate(feature = factor(feature, levels = features),
         outcome = factor(rise, levels = 0:1, labels = c("fell next year", "rose next year"))) |>
  ggplot(aes(outcome, value, fill = outcome)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.size = 0.3, show.legend = FALSE) +
  facet_wrap(~feature, scales = "free_y", ncol = 4) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("fell next year" = "#2a6f97", "rose next year" = "#e76f51")) +
  labs(title = "Each feature for district-years that fell or rose next year (training rows)", x = NULL, y = NULL)
save_fig(p_box, "fig02_features_by_outcome", dir = paths$fig_rq3, height = 6, width = 8.5)
```

A simple way to measure how much each feature *on its own* separates rises from falls is its **AUC**: the
probability that a randomly chosen "rise" row has a higher value of the feature than a randomly chosen "fall" row.
0.5 means no separation. Values below 0.5 mean the feature separates in the other direction (lower values go with
rises), so we also show max(AUC, 1 − AUC).

```{r univariate}
uni <- tibble(feature = features) |>
  mutate(auc = map_dbl(feature, \(v) auc(rq3$rise[rq3$split == "train"], rq3[[v]][rq3$split == "train"])),
         separation = pmax(auc, 1 - auc),
         direction = if_else(auc > 0.5, "higher → rise", "higher → fall")) |>
  arrange(desc(separation))
save_tab(uni, "t01_univariate_auc", dir = paths$tab_rq3) |>
  kable(digits = 3, caption = "Single-feature AUC on the training rows")
```

**Observation.** No single feature separates rises from falls well: the best AUC is about 0.62, where 0.5 is
guessing. The strongest signals are:

* **End-of-year momentum**, nationally (`nat_h2_vs_h1`) and in the district (`h2_vs_h1`). If the second half of the
  year was busier than the first, next year tends to be higher.
* **The national level vs its five-year average** (`nat_dev_5y`). Higher goes with rising, so the national cycle
  shows momentum over a one-year horizon.
* **Building intensity and the multi-unit share** point the other way: districts already building a lot per
  resident, or relying on apartment and townhouse projects, are slightly more likely to fall next year.
* The district's **own growth this year** (`growth_1y`, `dev_5y`) has a weak *negative* link: a district that
  jumped this year is slightly more likely to fall back next year (mean reversion), while the national series shows
  momentum.

The signal is weak but consistent. Step 2 will show how much the models can combine it.

# Overlap between features (correlation and VIF)

Logistic regression and LDA are both linear models, and their coefficients become unstable when features overlap.
We check the variance inflation factor (VIF = 1 / (1 − R²) from regressing each feature on the others; see RQ2
Step 1).

```{r vif}
vif_rq3 <- function(df) map_dbl(names(df), function(v)
  1 / (1 - summary(lm(reformulate(setdiff(names(df), v), v), data = df))$r.squared)) |> set_names(names(df))
train_x <- rq3 |> filter(split == "train") |> select(all_of(features))
vif_all <- vif_rq3(train_x)
tibble(feature = names(vif_all), vif = vif_all) |> arrange(desc(vif)) |> kable(digits = 2, caption = "VIF, all twelve features")
round(cor(train_x$growth_1y, train_x$growth_2y), 2)
```

**Observation.** No feature reaches the usual warning level of 5. The highest are `dev_5y` (4.6) and `growth_2y`
(3.7). These three growth measures overlap by construction: `growth_2y` is this year's growth plus last year's, and
both are part of `dev_5y`. `growth_2y` is also the weakest feature on its own (AUC 0.51). We drop it, which brings
every VIF below 3 and leaves eleven features.

```{r vif-final}
features_final <- setdiff(features, "growth_2y")
vif_final <- vif_rq3(train_x |> select(all_of(features_final)))
tibble(feature = names(vif_final), vif = vif_final) |> arrange(desc(vif)) |>
  save_tab("t02_vif", dir = paths$tab_rq3) |> kable(digits = 2, caption = "VIF, final eleven features")
```

# Save

```{r save}
rq3_model <- rq3 |>
  select(ta, region, island, is_city, year, split, rise, dwellings, next_dwellings, nat_rise_next,
         all_of(features)) |>
  mutate(rise_f = factor(rise, levels = 0:1, labels = c("fall", "rise")))
saveRDS(list(data = rq3_model, features = features_final, all_features = features,
             forecast = forecast |> select(ta, region, island, is_city, year, dwellings, all_of(features))),
        file.path(paths$processed, "rq3_model_data.rds"))
write_csv(rq3_model, file.path(paths$processed, "rq3_model_data.csv"))
dim(rq3_model)
```

# Summary of decisions

| # | Decision | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | One row per district and calendar year; 66 districts | The question is about next year; Chatham Islands too small |
| 2 | Label = new dwellings next year > this year (ties = not rising) | The headline count; ties are under 2% |
| 3 | Features use only information available at the end of year *t* | The model must be usable at the time of prediction |
| 4 | Feature years 1996–2024; train 1996–2016, test 2017–2024 | Five years of history for `dev_5y`; `dwell_per_1000` starts in 1996; time-ordered test |
| 5 | National features included | Districts move with the national cycle |
| 6 | Drop `growth_2y` | Overlaps `growth_1y` and `dev_5y` and adds nothing on its own (AUC 0.51) |

**Next (Step 2):** fit and compare classifiers (baselines, logistic regression, LDA, QDA, a
classification tree, k-nearest neighbours, lasso logistic regression and a random forest), tuned by time-ordered
cross-validation and tested once on 2017–2024.
